title: The Dancer Upstairs
full_review:
A methodical police detective pursues the leader of a terrorist organization threatening to bring down a Latin American country in the low-key thriller, "The Dancer Upstairs" (Fox Searchlight).

Actor John Malkovich makes an effectively understated debut as a director with this timely tale of corruption and terrorism, which is based on the early 1990s pursuit of the leader of Peru's revolutionary Shining Path movement.

Javier Bardem portrays Rejas, a corporate lawyer so turned off by corruption he becomes a policeman hoping to make a difference. Rejas is put in charge of a small group of dedicated cops after ritualistic animal killings around the country escalate to bombings and murders. All they have to go on is the name the terrorist leader is using: Ezequiel.

At home Rejas stifles his boredom with his vain and air-headed wife (Alexandra Lencastre). In taking his young daughter to ballet classes, he finds himself unwillingly drawn to her teacher, Yolanda (Laura Morante). He avoids revealing to her that he is with the police or on the trail of the country's most wanted man.

When military and government leaders are assassinated, martial law is declared and the hunt taken from his supervision. With political corruption all around him, Rejas continues digging for the whereabouts of the concealed guerrilla leader, appalled at how even young schoolgirls have been enlisted as suicide bombers. His concern becomes even more personal when the ballet school where Yolanda lives and his daughter attends classes is thought to be exactly where Ezequiel is hiding.

Based on Nicholas Shakespeare's novel and screenplay, the film manages the feat of being a methodical police procedural that is quietly riveting. Much of this can be credited to Bardem's perfectly pitched performance as his frustrated cop stoically endures personal and career setbacks while never losing track of his need to capture the terrorist. Morante as well gives a silky performance as the dancer who finds Rejas intriguing but is holding secrets of her own. Their relationship does not typically head for the bedroom, but to a series of choices that defines their destinies.

What lifts the film above the typical thriller action-film genre is the nuanced narrative that exposes the violence on both sides, not only of the revolutionaries but by government and military officials wielding power with scant regard for the citizenry. Rejas' struggle with marital fidelity and determination to remain uncorruptable also give the drama a thoughtful and welcome moral sensibility.

Although sluggishly paced, Malkovich uses on-location sites in Spain, Portugal and Ecuador effectively, with carefully composed shots and angles creating an ominous atmosphere of constant danger. The bloodbath scene where young schoolgirls set off bombs is as ugly as the work of callous real-life terrorists. And the bittersweet ending suggests that this is a war that will never be neatly won and confined to reports in history books.

Smart and serious, "The Dancer Upstairs" has at times a mournful tone that makes one want to offer up a prayer for all the world's victims of terrorism.

Due to some intense violence with gore, flash of nudity and fleeting sexual reference, intermittent rough language and occasional profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
